title: Retrieval Timing, Failure Diagnosis and Authoritative Sources

concepts.heading: Pre-inference versus just-in-time retrieval
concepts.body: Retrieval can run at two moments, and the exam asks you to pick one for a use case. Pre-inference retrieval means the application queries the index before the model call and places the chunks in the prompt. It always happens, costs one model call and gives predictable latency. Just-in-time (JIT) agentic retrieval means the agent holds a retriever tool and decides during its run whether, when and what to search. Be precise about the source of these names: the Databricks docs describe the mechanisms but do not define the two terms, so they are the exam guide's vocabulary and generally accepted practice. The documented mechanism for JIT is a retriever tool such as VectorSearchRetrieverTool from AI Bridge, which exposes an AI Search index as a tool, with a description that tells the agent when to search. Pick pre-inference when every request needs the same source and grounding is mandatory. Pick JIT when the next lookup depends on what the last one found, as with a coding agent exploring files. JIT costs extra model round trips and relies on the model choosing to search.

concepts.heading: Deciding per context element, not per agent
concepts.body: The choice is made for each context element, so one agent can use both timings. Facts that are always needed, small and fetched by a known key, such as a caller's plan, contract date and open case, are cheap and certain to be required. Load them before inference and skip a model round trip. Knowledge whose need depends on how the conversation unfolds, such as which article fits a diagnosis the agent has not reached yet, belongs behind a retriever tool. Loading those articles up front would usually fetch irrelevant text, because the first message rarely reveals the diagnosis, and irrelevant text dilutes the facts that matter. Two traps appear on the exam. Putting a mandatory behavior behind a tool is one: a stronger prompt only lowers the chance of skipping, so if citations are required on every answer, retrieve in application code before inference. That also puts a RETRIEVER span in every traced run, so retrieval judges can score every run. The other trap is loading everything into the prompt, which spends the attention budget on text that is mostly irrelevant.

concepts.heading: Reading a retrieval failure from eval logs
concepts.body: When answers are wrong, read the judge scores together with the retrieval spans. MLflow 3 built-in judges score retrieval separately. RetrievalRelevance asks whether the retrieved context is relevant to the request. RetrievalGroundedness asks whether the response is grounded in that context. RetrievalSufficiency asks whether the context contains what the ground-truth expectations need, so it requires expectations, as does Correctness. A retrieval span is a RETRIEVER span whose output is a list of documents, which makes the retrieved content inspectable. The failure names below are the exam's convention, not a Databricks taxonomy. High relevance with low sufficiency means on-topic text that lacks the needed content: the authoritative source is probably not in the corpus, and Unity Catalog metadata showing what feeds the index confirms it. Sufficient but ungrounded points at the prompt or model. Chunk size, a reranker or a larger candidate pool cannot supply text that is absent, so the governance action is to onboard the missing source to the indexed corpus.

concepts.heading: Constraining retrieval to authoritative sources
concepts.body: Unity Catalog lets stewards flag assets with the system.certification_status tag, whose values are certified and deprecated. Setting it needs ASSIGN on that governed tag, plus ownership of the object or APPLY TAG, USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG. The docs describe the tag as a signal of trust or lifecycle. They do not say it blocks queries, so a certified label alone does not stop an agent from reading an uncertified staging table. Enforcement comes from what the retriever is built on and from grants. A pre-deployment strategy, which is a practice rather than a documented procedure, has three steps: curate approved documents in one governed location, certify them and deprecate superseded copies, then build the AI Search index only from that source and grant the agent's service principal only what it needs. Databricks recommends least privilege and a dedicated service principal per app, so a permission error on an unapproved source is the control working. As a practice, limit ASSIGN on the tag to stewards so teams cannot certify their own copies, and separate corpora by audience. Check evaluation-trace documents before release. Prompt rules are not access controls.

examPoints: Pre-inference versus JIT retrieval are the exam's terms, not Databricks-defined: choose pre-inference when every request needs the source and grounding is mandatory, JIT when the next lookup depends on the previous result.

Read judge scores with retrieval spans: high RetrievalRelevance with low RetrievalSufficiency and a source missing from the index means onboard the authoritative asset; chunking or reranking cannot add absent text.
The certification tag is a label, not enforcement: constrain retrieval by curating and certifying, building the index from the approved source and scoping the service principal's grants.

quiz.q: A refund-policy chatbot must ground every answer in one policy index, and the team wants one model call per question with predictable latency. Which design fits?
choices: Give the agent a retriever tool and instruct it in the system prompt to always search before answering
Query the index in application code before the model call and place the top chunks in the prompt
Let the agent answer first, then run a second call that retrieves evidence and corrects the answer
Place the complete policy library in the system prompt so no retrieval step is needed at all
quiz.explain: The application queries the index on every request, so retrieval always happens and one model call is enough. A prompt instruction only lowers the chance of skipping, a post-answer pass adds a call and lets ungrounded text escape, and the full library wastes attention budget.

quiz.q: An agent's service principal holds SELECT on a whole catalog. The steward certified the approved tables, yet a trace shows the agent returning rows from an uncertified staging table. What is the right conclusion and fix?
choices: The tag is only a label and does not block reads, so scope the grants and retrieval source to certified assets
Certification changes are slow to take effect, so wait for the tag to propagate across the metastore before testing again
Certification should be reapplied to the staging table so the agent will treat it as the approved source from now on
Certification can be enforced by naming the tag in the system prompt and telling the agent to obey it strictly
quiz.explain: The tag signals trust but does not stop queries; the broad SELECT still permits staging reads. Limiting grants and building the retriever from certified assets creates the boundary. Waiting, tagging the staging table or naming the tag in a prompt enforces nothing.

recap: Pick pre-inference retrieval when grounding is mandatory and the source is fixed, JIT when needs are unpredictable. Diagnose with judges and retrieval spans, fix missing sources in the corpus, and enforce authority with certification plus scoped grants.

title: Memory Types, Delta-Backed State and Retrieving Memories

concepts.heading: Matching the memory type to the information need
concepts.body: Databricks documents two managed stores, both backed by Lakebase and usable from agents built on any framework. Agent sessions hold the state of one interaction, most commonly the ordered transcript of messages, tool calls and results, but also any state a framework persists, such as a LangGraph graph. Agent memory holds durable facts, preferences and decisions that the agent recalls in later, separate conversations, retrieved by semantic search. A session is scoped to one interaction; a memory is scoped to a subject, such as a user. The docs say to use both together for most cases, sessions alone for in-interaction state, and memory alone when the framework already manages session state. Diagnose a mismatch with one test: must the information still be available after this conversation ends and a different one begins? If yes, it needs memory. If it only matters while the chat continues, the session already covers it, and a window that fills during one long task is a within-conversation problem for trimming or compaction, not for adding long-term memory. Short-term versus long-term memory is general agent vocabulary.

concepts.heading: Episodic and derived memory
concepts.body: The stateful-agents page says Databricks memory research describes the same architecture with different terms. The session store holds episodic memory, the raw record of each session. The memory store holds derived memory, the facts and workflows distilled from those sessions. A memory pipeline is the offline process, called the dreaming process, that reads sessions, extracts durable facts, writes them to the memory store and consolidates them over time, on demand or on a schedule. This matters for context because recalled memory enters the window. Raw episodic records spend attention budget on greetings and repeated text, while distilled facts carry the signal in few tokens. The layers also serve different needs: a compliance team wanting a complete, replayable record reads sessions, while personalization reads memory. The stores are independent, so deleting a session, or an entire session store, does not delete memories already retained in the memory store. Removing a memory therefore means acting on the memory store itself.

concepts.heading: Delta-backed state object versus in-context scratchpad
concepts.body: A scratchpad is working notes kept inside the context window, such as a plan or a running list. It is a generally accepted agent term, not a Databricks-documented feature, and the exam uses it for state that lives only in context. It is cheap and has no read or write latency, so it is enough when state is needed only until the turn or task ends, losing it costs a retry rather than wrong side effects, and it is small. It fails for long or shared work. Notes disappear with the window on a restart, can be summarized away by compaction, cost attention on every turn, and can pile up stale entries that distract the model. Delta-backed state object is the exam's term for a plain Delta table in Unity Catalog, with no Preview feature involved. It is durable, queryable with SQL and shared by every run or agent. Use it for multi-day workflows, parallel agents that must see each other's progress, auditable records, and exact counters or positions. The agent reads only the row it needs and writes status back.

concepts.heading: Structured query or AI Search over stored memories
concepts.body: Lakebase is managed Postgres, so ordinary SQL, keys and indexes apply to records you keep in your own tables there. A structured query returns exact values deterministically when the agent knows the key and the field, such as a customer's current plan tier, a count over a date range or a record with a known identifier. Semantic search, through Databricks AI Search or the semantic recall of agent memory, ranks by similarity of meaning and suits free-text recall where the user paraphrases, because an embedding can match a note about anxiety to a question about stress. Equality and LIKE filters fail on paraphrase. Identifiers such as SKUs carry little semantic signal, and the docs say AI Search hybrid keyword-similarity search, which merges vector and keyword results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, helps where data has unique keywords. Ownership is a predicate, not a similarity: scope a shared store with a metadata filter on the query or a WHERE clause so other customers' rows never become candidates. A prompt or score threshold is not that control.

examPoints: Sessions are scoped to one interaction, memory to a subject; use memory only when information must survive into a separate conversation, and fix a filling window with trimming or compaction.
Use a Delta-backed state object (a plain Unity Catalog table) when state must survive restarts, be shared across agents, be audited or stay exact; a scratchpad suffices for small, short-lived state.
Structured SQL for known keys, columns and aggregates; semantic search for paraphrased free text; hybrid search for identifiers inside prose; a filter, not a prompt, for tenant scope.

quiz.q: A travel agent's framework checkpointer already persists each chat so it resumes after a restart. Travelers complain that a seat preference stated in one chat is unknown in a later chat. What is the mismatch?
choices: The session store is too small, so the transcript should be extended to hold many more past chats at once
The context window is too short, so older turns of the current chat must be summarized and trimmed
There is in-interaction state but no durable, subject-scoped memory to carry facts across conversations
The agent should keep the preference in a scratchpad so that it is repeated in each and every new chat
quiz.explain: The gap is cross-conversation recall, which memory scoped to a subject covers. A larger session or summaries only help within one interaction, and a scratchpad lives in the window and disappears with it.

quiz.q: A support agent stores customer facts as rows in Lakebase Postgres. A user asks, "What is my current plan tier?" and the tier is one column on the customer row. Which retrieval fits?
choices: A SQL lookup on the customer key for the exact value
A similarity search over embedded notes, ranked by closeness of meaning to the question asked
A hybrid keyword-similarity query, merged by Reciprocal Rank Fusion, over free-text notes about the customer
A language-model summary of the full history, trusted to mention the current tier correctly
quiz.explain: When the key and field are known, a structured query is exact and cheap. Similarity ranking adds uncertainty for a single column value, and summaries may omit it.

recap: Choose the store by scope (interaction or subject), move durable multi-step state into Delta tables rather than the window, and match retrieval to the query: SQL for exact fields, semantic search for paraphrase, filters for ownership.

title: Comparing Runs, Static versus Dynamic Retrieval, Over- and Under-Retrieval

concepts.heading: Choosing the most reliable configuration in MLflow 3
concepts.body: mlflow.genai.evaluate() runs an app over an evaluation dataset with scorers, such as LLM judges and code checks, and records one trace per row with feedback in an evaluation run. The docs tutorial compares versions in the experiment's Evaluation runs view: tick the runs, choose Compare from the Actions menu, and open the full traces for the same request from each run to see what each version put into the context. Reliability needs more than one mean. Model outputs vary between runs, so repeat the same dataset and scorers and weigh the spread against the average; treating the spread as a stability measure is generally accepted evaluation practice, not a Databricks rule. A high mean with a wide range depends on luck. A dataset can only show what it exercises: if every question is answerable from its own text, memory on and off will tie, so add rows whose answer depends on an earlier conversation. At equal quality, prefer the configuration that uses less context, because lower cost and latency and less distraction are real advantages.

concepts.heading: Static versus dynamic retrieval from Lakebase
concepts.body: Static and dynamic retrieval are the exam's vocabulary; the Databricks docs do not define them. Static retrieval means the application fetches a known, fixed piece of memory with a predetermined query before the model call and places it in the prompt. It is predictable and adds no model round trip. Dynamic retrieval means the model decides during the run to call a lookup tool and forms the query itself. It loads only what the task needs, but adds a tool-call round trip and depends on the model choosing to call it. Lakebase is managed Postgres, which suits a fixed keyed lookup before every request. The rule of thumb: always needed and small means static; sometimes needed, large or unpredictable means dynamic. Hybrid designs follow, loading a few stable fields such as segment or language every turn and leaving a large note history behind a tool. If traces show the agent skipping a dynamic lookup, the main lever is the tool description, which should say what the memory holds and which questions need it. Fields needed on nearly every call should become static.

concepts.heading: Over-retrieval and context pollution
concepts.body: Over-retrieval and under-retrieval are generally accepted retrieval terms and the exam's convention; the Databricks docs do not define them. Over-retrieval, also called context pollution, means too many or weakly relevant memories are injected. They spend the attention budget, distract the model, and let an old, unrelated fact steer the answer. Agent memory is retrieved by semantic search, so closest means most similar, not necessarily relevant, and a fixed count such as the 25 nearest memories always injects something even when only a few matter. In a trace the signs are many returned items with few used, an unrelated detail echoed in the answer, and prompt size that grows with the store. Pollution also comes from size, not only count: a memory entry that holds a whole transcript carries thousands of unrelated tokens around one useful sentence. Store one durable fact per entry (a design practice), since memory is meant for distilled facts and the raw record belongs in sessions. Other generally accepted fixes are a smaller cap, a relevance threshold and a query that states the current task.

concepts.heading: Under-retrieval and tuning both failures
concepts.body: Under-retrieval means a relevant memory exists in the store but never reaches the prompt, so the agent behaves as if it had forgotten. Typical causes are a similarity threshold so strict that a short query like what should I cook tonight never matches a stored sentence saying the user is vegetarian, a query that never mentions the constraint, and a cap so low that relevant items rank below it. Diagnose before changing anything by comparing three things in the trace: what the store contains, what retrieval returned and what the answer used. If the store has the fact but retrieval returns nothing, the gap is in retrieval. If the store lacks it, the gap is in writing, meaning the memory pipeline or the agent's memory writing. Lowering a cap trades one failure for the other, since a fixed small number cannot suit a question needing one fact and another needing three. Combine a relevance gate, which lets the count follow how many items are relevant, with a moderate cap, and rerun the same evaluation dataset and judges to confirm both improved.

examPoints: Compare MLflow 3 evaluation runs on the same dataset and scorers, look at spread as well as mean, and open traces to see the context; at equal quality pick the leaner configuration.

Static retrieval (fixed query before the call) suits small, always-needed memory; dynamic retrieval (a tool) suits large or rarely needed memory and depends on the tool description and the model's choice.
Over-retrieval is many items with few used; under-retrieval is a stored fact that never arrives. Fix with a relevance gate plus a moderate cap, one fact per entry, then re-evaluate both.

quiz.q: Three memory-injection configurations were each run five times in MLflow on the same dataset and judges. Configuration X has mean correctness 0.86 with scores from 0.84 to 0.88. Configuration Y has mean 0.88 with scores from 0.70 to 0.97. Configuration Z has mean 0.79 with scores from 0.78 to 0.80. Which is the most reliable, and why?
choices: Y, because the highest mean means it will be right most often in production
Z, because the narrowest range shows the most dependable behaviour of the three
Y, because its best single run shows the ceiling the configuration can reach
X, because a high mean with a narrow range is both strong and dependable
quiz.explain: Reliability weighs the spread against the mean. X is nearly as accurate as Y and far more stable, while Z is stable but lower. Y's wide range shows its result depends on the run.

quiz.q: An assistant injects the 25 closest memories from its Lakebase-backed memory store into every request. As the store grew, answers cited an irrelevant old fact. Which change best addresses the cause?
choices: Raise the cap to 50 so that the relevant memory is certain to be included every time
Remove the semantic search so memories are chosen at random for each request
Add a relevance gate and moderate cap, then rerun the same evaluation
Switch to a model with a larger window so that all 25 memories fit comfortably
quiz.explain: The symptom is over-retrieval: weakly relevant items fill the window. A relevance gate lets the count follow relevance, a cap bounds the worst case, and the rerun checks that recall did not drop. More items or a bigger window keep the distraction.

recap: Judge configurations on mean and spread with traces, match static or dynamic retrieval to how predictable the need is, and tune over- and under-retrieval together with a relevance gate, a moderate cap and one fact per memory.

title: Durable Memory across Sessions and Resolving Intent before Retrieval

concepts.heading: Configuring persistent memory across sessions
concepts.body: The stateful-agents page lists the pieces you configure. A session store keeps each interaction's state. A memory store holds durable facts. A memory pipeline reads the conversations in the session store, extracts durable facts, writes them to the memory store, on demand or on a schedule, and consolidates them over time, without adding memory-writing tools to your agent. The tutorial on adding sessions and memory to an existing agent connects those three; the Agent Bricks quickstart builds a new agent with them already set up. Consolidation matters because recall is semantic search: if a nightly pipeline writes forty near-identical entries for one preference, they all score high and occupy every slot of a small result list, pushing a different relevant fact out. Merge duplicates at write time so each slot carries a different fact. Because the stores are independent, a retired agent's session store can be deleted without losing the memories, and clearing a memory is a separate action. Managed agent memory governed by Unity Catalog is documented as Legacy and not recommended for new agents, so it is never the answer for a new design.

concepts.heading: Subject scope and store permissions
concepts.body: Memory is scoped to a subject, not an interaction. A common bug is keying memories by the current chat identifier. A fact then behaves like session state and can only be found from the chat that created it, so a size preference set on Monday is unknown in Wednesday's new chat. The docs state the scoping. Treating each customer as a subject, written and recalled by that subject so one customer's memories never reach another, is a design practice built on it. Databricks documents permissions for memory and session stores: you grant, inspect, list and revoke access to them. Two layers therefore exist. Store permissions decide which identities can read or write the stores at all. Subject-scoped recall, in practice, decides which memories a given request may see. Apply least privilege, granting only the agents and people who need a store and revoking when they no longer do. A prompt instruction such as only discuss this customer is not an access control, because the memories would already be in the model's context by the time the instruction is read.

concepts.heading: Where intent is resolved in the pipeline
concepts.body: Retrieval can only be as good as its query. A message like what did they decide about it has nothing an index can match, and embedding it raw returns noise. Resolving intent means turning the user message plus session state into a clear standalone query, and when needed choosing the source, before any retrieval runs. The stage is generally accepted pipeline vocabulary and the exam's convention; the Databricks docs do not define it. The order is: receive the message with session state, resolve intent by expanding references, disambiguating names and choosing between structured lookup and semantic search, retrieve with the resolved query, then inject the result. The session store is the natural input because it holds the conversation so far. Doing it after retrieval is too late, because the window already holds whatever the raw query matched. An ambiguous request such as the numbers for Apollo, where a project and a customer share the name, cannot be fixed by any retrieval setting; use session context or ask a short clarifying question rather than retrieving both meanings and inviting the model to blend them.

concepts.heading: Resolving intent only when it pays
concepts.body: Intent resolution costs a model call and latency, so apply it where it adds value. A self-contained message such as what is my current plan tier can be retrieved as written. A message with unresolved references, or one that could match several entities or sources, needs the step. A practical design puts a cheap check in front, either rules or a small classifier. Clear messages go straight to retrieval, and ambiguous ones are rewritten or answered with a clarifying question first. That keeps the benefits for the minority that needs them without taxing the majority; this is an engineering trade-off in the exam's convention, not a Databricks rule. The benefits when the step runs are two: a specific query retrieves less noise, so less attention budget is wasted and over-retrieval falls, and the resolved query can be routed to the method that fits, a structured query for a single stored field or semantic search for a vague recollection. It does not remove the need to evaluate retrieval or to store distilled memories.

examPoints: Persistent memory is session store plus memory store plus a memory pipeline that distills and consolidates; merge duplicates at write time and never choose the Legacy managed memory for a new agent.
Key memories by subject, not chat identifier; control access with store permissions and subject-scoped recall, not with prompt instructions.
Resolve intent after the message and session state arrive and before retrieval; it is the exam's term, and it can be skipped for self-contained messages to save a model call.

quiz.q: A shopping agent writes memories keyed by the current chat identifier. A customer sets a size preference on Monday, opens a new chat on Wednesday, and the agent asks for the size again. What is the fix?
choices: Scope memories to the customer as the subject, for writing and recalling alike
Extend the Monday session store so its transcript is replayed into every future chat automatically for the user
Increase the number of memories retrieved per request until the preference finally appears
Store the preference in a scratchpad inside the context window of each new chat the customer opens
quiz.explain: Memory is scoped to a subject, so keying by chat makes a durable fact behave like session state. A longer transcript, a bigger cap or a scratchpad does not give cross-conversation recall.

quiz.q: A support agent answers accurately but off target. A user writes "What did they decide about it?" after discussing a vendor contract earlier in the chat, and the pipeline embeds that raw sentence to query memory. Where should the fix go?
choices: After retrieval, with a reranker that reorders whatever the raw sentence happened to match
In a standalone query built from message and session state before retrieval
In the memory pipeline, which should store more entries so that the raw sentence matches them
In the system prompt, which should tell the agent to ignore any unrelated memories it receives
quiz.explain: Intent resolution belongs after the message and session state are available and before retrieval, so the query is clear. A reranker cannot recover content the raw query never matched, and the other two do not repair the query.

recap: Persistent memory needs sessions, a memory store and a pipeline that distills and consolidates; scope it by subject and permissions, and resolve intent into a clear query before retrieval, skipping the step for clear messages.
